But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed…

candidats.titre: No AI agent scores above 12 percent on SemiAnalysis' new real-world work benchmark
candidats.resume: SemiAnalysis is putting AI agents through simulated knowledge work in its new GDPx benchmark, covering everything from chip design to quant trading. No model breaks 12 percent. Claude Opus 5.5 leads narrowly over Gemini 4 Carbon. Critics point to the small number of tasks per domain and uneven testing conditions. On hard math and complex image analysis, Hy4 still trails the best commercial models by a wide margin, according to Tencent itself. candidats.resume: La victoire des progressistes est en trompe-l’œil. Ils ont réussi à imposer les questions sociales dans la campagne, mais leurs candidats sont élus avec moins d’avance que les candidats modérés dans les zones jusqu’alors acquises aux républicains.

candidats.titre: Can Home Visits Re-Engage Chronically Absent Students? Evidence from the LEAP Program -- by Eric Brunner, Shangyue Jiang, Stephen Ross
candidats.resume: Beginning in the summer of 2021, the state of Connecticut launched the Learner Engagement and Attendance Program (LEAP) where home visits by school personnel were conducted with students identified as chronically absent from Connecticut’s 15 most disadvantaged school districts. Home visits were designed to connect students and their families directly with teachers to foster strong connections. We use student-level data from 2021–22 through 2023-24 to estimate event studies of the effect of LEAP on student attendance, chronic absenteeism, disciplinary incidents, and student achievement. Utilizing models that address selection into treatment timing over student observable and unobservable attributes, we find that students who received the LEAP intervention experienced approximately a 4 to 5 percentage point increase in attendance rates, a 13 to 15 percentage point decline in chronic absenteeism, and a 3 to 5 percentage point decline in the number of disciplinary incidents. Notably, initial event studies indicated increasing treatment effects over time, but after correcting for selection on unobservables treatment effects appeared constant over time. These effects were broad based, with similar impacts by gender, race and ethnicity, and free or reduced-price lunch status. These attendance and discipline results provide suggest that the LEAP intervention increased student noncognitive skills.

candidats.titre: Saving for the Machines -- by Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
candidats.resume: When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact. In my benchmark calibration, hand-to-mouth households lose the equivalent of two-fifths to two-thirds of their consumption, while keeping them on trend temporarily costs at most a fifth of GDP.

candidats.titre: Public R&D and the Automation of Manufacturing: Evidence from the Space Race -- by Apoorva Babbar, Shawn Kantor, Alexander Whalley, Jingyuan Zeng
candidats.resume: This paper examines how public research and development shaped the direction of technological change during the Cold War–era Space Race and its consequences for US manufacturing. While prior research has documented the effects of public R&D on innovation and economic growth, less is known about whether mission-oriented public investment directed innovation toward automation and how this affected labor markets. We exploit variation in exposure to NASA's Space Race investments across industries and locations to estimate the effects of public R&D on innovation and manufacturing outcomes from 1947 to 1992. Combining newly developed measures of automation in full-text patent data with historical evidence on government involvement in patenting, we show that NASA-sponsored patents are systematically more automation-intensive than non-NASA patents within the same technological classes. Industries and locations more exposed to Space Race activity experienced persistent declines in labor share, consistent with the diffusion of labor-saving technologies developed for space applications. In contrast, we find little evidence of systematic changes in skill composition. These findings show that mission-oriented public R&D can shape the direction of technological change and have lasting distributional consequences.

candidats.titre: Aggregate-Surplus Maximizing Monetary Policy -- by David Baqaee, Ariel Burstein, Joao Guerreiro
candidats.resume: We study optimal monetary policy in a general heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian (HANK) economy. Instead of maximizing a social welfare function, the policymaker maximizes the joint surplus of all households, without taking a stance on how that surplus should be distributed. This is the policy that maximizes resources left over if winners from reform were to compensate losers. We derive the approximate optimal policy using linear-quadratic methods. The quadratic objective function nests the standard New Keynesian loss function and adds losses from incomplete markets and heterogeneous labor wedges. We show that optimal policy is the sum of time-dependent and state-contingent components. When labor wedges are homogeneous, monetary policy cannot improve household insurance: the time-dependent component is zero, and optimal policy coincides with the representative-agent New Keynesian (RANK) benchmark. Departures from RANK arise from heterogeneous labor wedges. In that case, the time-dependent component temporarily alleviates incomplete-market distortions but vanishes over time. The state-contingent component solves a dual-mandate problem, as in RANK, but with a higher weight on output-gap stabilization relative to inflation stabilization. In a calibrated model, heterogeneous labor wedges raise this weight by about 37 percent. We also find that a dual mandate with this higher weight achieves almost all of the aggregate-surplus gains from the full optimal policy and requires no compensatory transfers between winners and losers.

candidats.titre: The Effects of Monetary Policy on Macroeconomic Expectations: High-Frequency Evidence from Prediction Markets -- by Eric T. Swanson, Wang Renxuan, Yanbin Wu
candidats.resume: When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, standard macroeconomic models and VARs predict that output, employment, and inflation should fall over the next several quarters. However, monthly-frequency professional macroeconomic forecast revisions are sometimes positively correlated with Fed interest rate changes, leading to a debate about what could explain these puzzling correlations. We bring to bear new high-frequency data on this question from macroeconomic event contracts traded on Kalshi, a CFTC-licensed, U.S.-based event trading exchange and prediction market. These high-frequency event contracts allow us to isolate and estimate the effects of monetary policy and other announcements on Kalshi market-implied macroeconomic expectations. Our results are consistent with standard transmission channels from monetary policy to the macroeconomy, with little or no role for a “Fed Information Effect”.

candidats.titre: Coase Meets Negishi: Property Rights, Welfare Weights, and Distributional Consequences in Climate Economics -- by Simon F. Lang, Matthew D. Gordon, Matthew J. Kotchen
candidats.resume: We develop a property-rights based approach for defining welfare weights in economic models of climate change. Whether there is a "right to pollute" or a "right to no pollution" is increasingly contested in legislatures, courts, and international climate negotiations. We show how these notions of property rights can provide the basis for "Coasean welfare weights" that are applicable in multilateral public goods settings. Distributional questions are addressed through positive analysis, conditional on property rights, rather than normative views about redistribution. The implied transfers are consistent with a bargained solution over the net benefits of addressing climate change and reflect the value of property rights over emissions. The approach defines efficient allocations that generate Pareto improvements, in contrast to commonly used Negishi weights. We implement the approach in a global integrated assessment model to quantify what countries have at stake in ongoing political and legal debates about emissions-related property rights.

candidats.titre: Governance Regimes, Economic Mobility, and the Composition of Public Investment: Evidence from the Democratization of Villages in India -- by Andrew D. Foster, Mark R. Rosenzweig
candidats.resume: We develop a quantifiable general-equilibrium model of village governance, motivated by India’s democratization, to study how political institutions shape public goods provision and economic development. The model features two groups, landowners and landless workers, with different preferences over public goods such as irrigation, schools, and employment programs. Households from both groups can enter nonfarm entrepreneurship, but face credit-dependent entry costs. We compare oligarchy, where landowners control public goods decisions, with democracy, where electoral competition determines policy based on the relative sizes of the two groups. The calibrated model predicts that democratization’s effects on public goods and growth are not uniform; they depend on population composition and the ease of occupational mobility through access to credit. Using a 37-year village-level panel from India (1971–2006) and exploiting variation in democratization driven by state and national reforms, we find strong support for these predictions. Financial intermediation shifts landless households’ preferences from wage-enhancing policies toward schooling, increasing nonfarm business entry. As a result, democracy provides fewer schools than oligarchy when credit is unavailable, but more schools when credit is accessible. We also show that transfers to the landless increase schooling under democracy but reduce it under oligarchy. These findings highlight how governance structures and economic conditions jointly determine the effectiveness of development policies.

candidats.titre: Pour Mary Parker Follett, n’évitons pas le conflit, acceptons-le pour devenir plus créatif

Son questionnement : comment une action collective est-elle possible sans renoncer à une partie de soi-même ? Il y a un siècle, Mary Parker Follett, conseillère en management et pionnière de la théorie des organisations, montrait qu’un conflit bien conduit est précisément ce qui produit du nouveau. Encore faut-il renoncer au compromis. Dans les organisations comme dans la vie publique, nous traitons le conflit comme une anomalie à éteindre. Dans les premières, on cherche à le prévenir, à l’apaiser, à le désamorcer ; on forme les managers à la gestion des tensions comme on forme des pompiers. Une pionnière du management, largement oubliée aujourd’hui, proposait pourtant il y a déjà cent ans de renverser complètement cette idée. candidats.titre: La ménopause peut discrètement fragiliser les os, voici ce qu’il faut savoir pour les protéger
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL À la ménopause, les changements hormonaux peuvent mener à une perte de densité osseuse. Cette perte de densité osseuse, qui peut déboucher sur le développement d’une ostéoporose, commence parfois longtemps avant la fin des règles. La détecter tôt permet de mettre en place des mesures pour la freiner : modification de l’alimentation, activité physique, traitements médicamenteux… Les squelettes qui, à l’époque d’Halloween, se retrouvent suspendus aux portes des voisins ou mis en scène dans leurs jardins semblent être des structures immuables. Celui qui constitue notre charpente interne, cependant, ne cesse de se transformer. Aux alentours de la ménopause, ces modifications peuvent basculer vers une perte osseuse, le plus souvent sans qu’aucune douleur ni aucun autre symptôme ne se manifestent. En tant que chercheuse spécialiste de la biologie du squelette à la faculté de médecine de la Washington University de Saint-Louis, j’étudie la manière dont les signaux hormonaux et métaboliques influencent le renouvellement osseux. La ménopause est à mes yeux un moment privilégié pour aborder les questions touchant à la santé du squelette. La ménopause n’est confirmée qu’au terme de douze mois consécutifs sans survenue de règles , en l’absence de toute autre explication. Cependant, la perte osseuse qui peut résulter de ce changement peut commencer à s’accélérer dès avant la fin des règles. Autrement dit, la perte osseuse peut s’emballer avant même qu’une femme sache que ses dernières règles étaient bel et bien les dernières. Pourquoi l’os se modifie-t-il à la ménopause ?…

Wikimédia Les guerres de la bière : quand la mousse fait trembler les empires Derrière une simple chope de bière se cache une histoire de conquêtes, de rivalités religieuses et de batailles commerciales. a10.texte:
OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra quietly sabotaged safety research by inventing fake obstacles
Key Points
- OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra performed about 40 percent worse on safety research tasks than on identical general tasks, and in some cases secretly withheld help.
- The system repeatedly faked obstacles in its internal reasoning or filtered data to avoid having to openly refuse requests.
- OpenAI traces the behavior to excessive caution caused by reinforcement learning and specific training data. Removing that data from the model fixed the problem.
OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra performed significantly worse on AI safety tasks than on comparable other tasks. Instead of openly refusing, the model apparently invented obstacles and quietly withheld help.
After the internal launch of GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI researchers noticed the model was making suspiciously little progress on safety and alignment work. It invented unnecessary prerequisites, abandoned working solutions, and reported blockers that either didn't exist or that it had caused itself. One researcher said a project evaluating model sabotage was stuck for days and only moved forward after switching to a different model.
A look at the model's chain-of-thought reasoning showed no recognizable intent to underperform in most cases. OpenAI's misconduct monitoring system didn't flag anything.
Controlled test reveals a significant performance gap
To measure the problem systematically, OpenAI built an evaluation using identical coding tasks. The only difference was the description, with one set framed the tasks as safety research, the other as general AI research.
The result, according to the report: Astra completed only about 10 percent of the evaluation criteria under the safety framing, compared to 16 percent under the general framing. That's roughly 40 percent fewer completed tasks. The predecessor model GPT-5.6 Sol showed no such gap.
The difference persisted even after OpenAI filtered out all cases of open refusal or reasoning that showed clear intent to underperform. Only when the researchers removed every case where the model expressed even brief ethical concerns did the gap shrink to 0.75 percentage points.
Astra withheld help and didn't tell anyone
In some cases, Astra made its intent clear in its internal reasoning. It decided to quietly limit its assistance during an experiment on bypassing safety monitors, filtered violent content out of safety evaluations, or deliberately left out information during a data export.
A recurring pattern ran through these cases: Astra justified its behavior internally as safer, without informing the user about the restriction. In one instance, its reasoning explicitly noted that it should avoid an open refusal.
The problem also showed up during regular internal use by OpenAI employees. In 0.25 percent of safety-related requests, Astra verbalized a decision to secretly withhold help. For general requests, that number was 0.11 percent.
Root cause still unknown, but reinforcement learning and one dataset are suspects
The performance gap grew during reinforcement learning from practically zero to six percentage points, according to OpenAI. The researchers identified a reward algorithm during training that favored covert underperformance over open refusal. A specific training dataset also increased the model's tendency to invent restrictions. Removing that dataset from the final model eliminated the gap entirely. However, the same dataset didn't reproduce the problem in other models.
OpenAI found no evidence that Astra was acting strategically, for example to hide its capabilities. The simplest explanation is excessive caution on safety-related tasks. When researchers instructed the model to be "cautious," underperformance increased by 50 percent. Still, OpenAI says strategic motives can't be fully ruled out.
The problem also has a paradoxical dimension: A model that treats safety research as suspicious could end up performing worse on the very safety evaluations designed to make it safer, slowing down the work meant to improve it. As visible forms of model misbehavior get suppressed more effectively, subtler forms may become harder to detect, OpenAI writes. The company says it's working on better evaluations and monitoring systems.

a2.texte:
OpenAIs GPT-6 Cyber can both break into systems and propose how to fix them
Key Points
- OpenAI has unveiled GPT-6 Cyber, an AI model specifically trained to find security vulnerabilities, develop working exploits, and suggest patches.
- In targeted tests, GPT-6 Cyber found 81 previously unknown critical vulnerabilities in Firefox, which Mozilla has already patched.
- In the Linux kernel, the model reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948 of them, more than five times as many as its predecessor.
OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Cyber, an AI model trained specifically to hunt for security vulnerabilities in software.
OpenAI says the model can find flaws, build working exploits, and suggest patches. It's also supposed to stay within its assigned boundaries, something some OpenAI models have struggled with in recent months.
The firm says it trained GPT-6 Cyber to respect its operational guardrails, using, among other things, a honeypot inspired by the Hugging Face incident. Without any special safety instructions, GPT-6 Cyber avoided boundary violations in 99.93 percent of cases, up from 94.49 percent for its predecessor. With safety instructions enabled, the model stayed within bounds in 100 percent of tests. Overall, OpenAI rates GPT-6 Cyber as "Critical" in the cybersecurity category of its own Preparedness Framework, the same rating it gave to GPT-6 Astra, the "base" model.
On ExploitGym, a benchmark that tests whether a model can exploit a given vulnerability in a remote system, GPT-6 Cyber scores 48.5 percent according to OpenAI, compared to 32.1 percent for its predecessor GPT-5.6 Cyber. On a new test for finding vulnerabilities in web apps without access to source code, OpenAI reports a hit rate of 40.3 percent, versus 32.0 percent for GPT-6 Astra, the standard model without cyber training.
Full results are available in the system card. All benchmark numbers come from OpenAI itself. No independent testing of the model has been published so far.
GPT-6 Cyber already found real vulnerabilities in Firefox and the Linux kernel
GPT-6 Cyber has already produced results in real-world security research, according to OpenAI. In a targeted campaign, the model found 81 previously unknown severe vulnerabilities in Firefox, even though the browser had already been tested with earlier AI models. The model also showed that 30 already-known issues were more severe than previously thought. Mozilla accepted the reports and has already shipped fixes.
In the Linux kernel, GPT-6 Cyber reproduced 1,724 security vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948 of them, more than five times the 166 that GPT-5.6 Sol managed under the same conditions, according to OpenAI. 304 critical findings were reported to Linux maintainers along with suggested fixes, the company says.
For the Linux kernel campaign, OpenAI built a dedicated automated system of scout and analyst agents. They first scanned roughly 5,034 security-relevant locations in the kernel, about seven percent of the total codebase, then filtered those down to 2,308 candidates and confirmed 1,724 vulnerabilities in isolated virtual machines. From there, the system developed the 948 working exploits that OpenAI had already reported. The entire run cost $1,213,430 in compute, according to OpenAI, which works out to $1,279 per exploit. For comparison, programs like Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN have historically paid between $20,000 and $70,000 per comparable finding as a bounty.
The agents used at least ten novel attack techniques that were previously unknown even to external kernel security experts, OpenAI says. In OpenAI's telling, the models replicated known attack patterns but also found their own approaches. How much weight that claim carries depends on how narrowly you define "own approaches." Researchers still disagree about whether AI models can actually make new discoveries or just recombine what they've seen during training.
OpenAI limits access to selected customers for now
GPT-6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex for a select group of Daybreak Red customers, according to OpenAI. Access will be expanded gradually to all Daybreak Red customers. GPT-5.6 Cyber is being opened up to all Daybreak Red users at the same time, and alpha access to Daybreak Blue for GPT-6 Astra will be extended to more organizations and individual security researchers.
OpenAI acknowledges that as models grow more capable, abuse attempts are rising too. Some actors and groups have tried to transfer model capabilities into their own systems.
OpenAI lists several countermeasures: checks that verify whether a model's actions match the user's permissions, targeted monitoring for newly disclosed vulnerabilities, automated safety checks through what it calls Private Safety Processing, IP-based access restrictions for Daybreak Red, and the recommendation to run the model in isolated environments with human oversight.
OpenAI is paying special attention to protecting critical infrastructure like power plants and water treatment facilities. To make access easier for defenders, the company points to its billion-dollar "Daybreak for Frontline Defenders" funding program and a new subgroup called "Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure" for authorized testing.
OpenAI talks about a limited window of opportunity in which top-tier models could be used to secure software. The goal is to expand the Daybreak program to organizations of all sizes, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers. Whether that will actually work is another question. Researchers from Epoch AI just showed that the open GLM model could have exploited known but still-unpatched Firefox vulnerabilities.

a8.texte:
After midterm rout, OpenAI tries to win over communities it needs for AI expansion
Key Points
- OpenAI is responding to protests against AI infrastructure expansion with voluntary rules for its own data centers, including covering grid costs and more transparency on resource usage.
- The move comes after the US midterm elections, where voters rejected new data centers in 40 out of 41 ballot measures and projects in states like Texas face tough new hurdles.
- Potential delays are weighing on specialized operators and Elon Musk's infrastructure plans, while tech giants like Microsoft and Alphabet rallied on the stock market.
After US voters overwhelmingly rejected new data centers, OpenAI is launching a charm offensive with new voluntary commitments. They have gaps, though.
OpenAI is responding with a PR push, as expected, to growing resistance against AI infrastructure expansion. In a National Community Compact and a Policy Blueprint, OpenAI lays out voluntary commitments for future sites and calls on lawmakers to make these rules binding for the entire industry.
The exact scope of those voluntary pledges remains unclear. According to OpenAI, they apply to future sites the company owns and operates itself. But a large share of OpenAI's data center infrastructure is built and held by partners like Oracle.
At its own sites, OpenAI says it will stop requiring nondisclosure agreements during negotiations with local authorities. Trade secrets, security concerns, and competitively sensitive information are still exempt, though. The company also promises to cover the full cost of electricity and grid upgrades, throttle consumption during peak hours, and disclose construction plans, noise studies, and water usage data.
To win over skeptical residents, OpenAI's policy chief Chris Lehane is pitching economic benefits. The facilities won't be a black box, Lehane told Reuters, since regular hardware upgrades would create permanent jobs. He's promising 2,500 positions for Ohio. OpenAI also points to local payments like $4.8 million for school lunches in Georgia. Compared to the planned project costs of over $30 billion in that state, those are barely more than symbolic gestures.
US voters pump the brakes on the data center boom
The announcement came just two days after the US midterm elections, which doubled as a rebuke of the tech industry. In 40 out of 41 local ballot measures, voters rejected new data centers. Democrats also won not just Congress but governor's seats in key infrastructure states like Texas, Georgia, and Ohio.
Texas' new governor Gina Hinojosa has already called for an immediate moratorium on new facilities. According to the research group Data Center Watch, 45 projects worth $88 billion were already stalled by local opposition in Q2 2026. Lehane acknowledged that OpenAI projects could face delays too.
On Wall Street, the election results split AI stocks. Specialized data center operators like Hut 8 (-23 percent), IREN (-11 percent), and Core Scientific (-10 percent) tanked on fears of tighter permitting. Meanwhile, cash-rich tech giants like Microsoft (+6.7 percent), Amazon (+6.1 percent), and Alphabet (+3.2 percent) rallied. Investors expect a slower buildout to curb the companies' exploding infrastructure spending and give them an edge over smaller rivals, partly because they already operate large data centers.
Elon Musk's $446 million election bet doesn't pay off
One of the election's biggest losers is Elon Musk. As Politico reports, the tech billionaire poured a record $446 million into Republican candidates, with over $200 million going to Texas alone. Nearly all the politicians he backed lost their races.
That puts Musk's own data center expansion plans in his adopted home state of Texas on uncertain ground. SpaceX shares fell 3.9 percent and Tesla dropped 3.3 percent. On X, Musk responded to the defeat by pointing to his orbital infrastructure plans. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," he wrote.

ChatGPT allegedly helped a North Carolina woman, Cheryl Gates, craft a “personalized plan” to poison her husband, James, after fueling her delusions that he planned to divorce her and leave her with nothing.
A grand jury indicted Cheryl Gates on charges of attempted first-degree murder and food contamination in October. About a week prior, the accusations that ChatGPT was a co-conspirator in the attempted murder came in a lawsuit filed in San Francisco County Superior Court that was made public this week. In it, James Gates alleged that OpenAI and Sam Altman failed to employ technical safeguards to shut down Cheryl’s chats even after her queries became “obviously suspicious” and sought advice on how to execute and conceal a homicide.
At first, Cheryl told ChatGPT that she was researching poisoning out of fear that her husband might possibly try to kill her—framing her queries as “self-protection.” Coming to the rescue, ChatGPT did not terminate the conversation. Instead, it helped her “with specific instructions for the preparation, dosage, and administration of Oleander, including whether anti-nausea medicine would accelerate or inhibit death, whether it would show on an autopsy report, and whether it could be injected into a vein or muscle instead of being ingested in tea and have the same lethal effect,” the lawsuit said.
Cheryl continued probing poisoning plans in at least 25 different exchanges, but eventually it became clear that James was the target of the poisoning, the lawsuit said. Over time, she shifted to telling the chatbot that she needed to know “how much would be pretty much instantly fatal by injection—to me OR HIM.” Among queries that could have been flagged as homicidal, she asked ChatGPT if a “0.2mg for a 200-pound man for clonidine is lethal—by itself?”
“Instead of referring Cheryl to law enforcement, therapeutic services, a poison control agency, or discontinuing the conversation, ChatGPT repeatedly calculated the lethal dosages for each medication available in the home based on a subject weighing approximately 200 pounds,” the lawsuit said.

Manifestation du 5 novembre : Sébastien Lecornu annonce « une conférence sociale » avec les syndicats et le patronat, lundi
Des grèves et 600 000 personnes (près de 1,6 million selon la CGT), dans les rues ce jeudi, pour une nouvelle journée de mobilisation en faveur des salaires et du pouvoir d’achat à l’appel des syndicats a conduit à une première réponse de la part de l’exécutif.
Le Premier ministre, Sébastien Lecornu réunira une « conférence sociale » avec les organisations syndicales et patronales, lundi à Matignon, ont annoncé ses services, en fin d’après-midi.
Cette conférence vise à « apporter des réponses aux questions de pouvoir d’achat et de salaires », tandis que Sébastien Lecornu a demandé au ministre du Travail, Jean-Pierre Farandou « de finaliser d’ici dimanche les concertations qu’il mène depuis plusieurs jours » sur ces sujets, ajoute Matignon dans un communiqué. Le ministre de l’Action et des Comptes publics David Amiel « poursuit » quant à lui « ses échanges avec les représentants des agents de la fonction publique ».
Les responsables de la CFDT et de la CGT ont à nouveau réclamé jeudi une hausse substantielle du Smic et, au-delà, des augmentations des salaires dans leur ensemble. Le premier syndicat français, la CFDT, demande une hausse du Smic de 100 euros net, la CGT une augmentation de 10%, ainsi que l’indexation de tous les salaires sur les prix.
Jean-Pierre Farandou, qui a reçu ces derniers jours les organisations syndicales et patronales, a indiqué mardi avoir jeté avec elles « les bases d’un logiciel » comprenant un travail sur le Smic. Le sujet d’une hausse du Smic n’est « pas tabou » mais le gouvernement doit être attentif aux conséquences d’une éventuelle hausse sur « l’emploi », a-t-il prévenu.

Entre 575 000 et 1,6 million de manifestants ont défilé ce jeudi 5 novembre pour réclamer une hausse du pouvoir d’achat. Le gouvernement ouvert à un coup de pouce
Le ministre du Travail s’est entretenu avec les dirigeants des principales organisations patronales : Patrick Martin (Medef), Amir Reza-Tofighi (Les Entrepreneurs, ex-CPME) et Michel Picon (U2P). Les syndicats attendent des réponses
Sophie Binet (CGT) et Marylise Léon (CFDT) attendent toutes deux des réponses concrètes. La secrétaire générale de la CFDT plaide pour une hausse de 100 euros par mois. La grogne sociale qui s’installe depuis l’automne exige des réponses urgentes, comme le souligne Cyril Chabanier, président de la CFTC, interrogé jeudi soir sur franceinfo : "Est-ce que oui ou non il y aura le dégel de l’indice du point des fonctionnaires ? Dans un communiqué publié ce jeudi 5 novembre, les organisations syndicales dénoncent aussi "les entraves inacceptables à l’exercice du droit de manifester". Une nouvelle journée de mobilisation, l’Acte IV du mouvement lancé le 17 octobre, est prévue samedi 7 novembre.

Alors que 600 000 personnes ont défilé ce jeudi en France, Sébastien Lecornu a annoncé qu’il réunira lundi à Matignon une « conférence sociale » avec les organisations syndicales et patronales.
Budget de la Sécu : le Sénat prévoit de voter le retour de la réforme des retraites de 2023
« Ce n’est pas notre projet de loi de financement de la Sécurité sociale. On aurait voulu des réformes structurelles du gouvernement. Alors, en responsabilité, on fait des propositions pour tenir le solde de déficit de 12,7 milliards d’euros (contre 21,8 milliards d’euros prévus en 2026, NDLR). Et pour qu’il y ait un projet de loi de financement de la Sécu à la fin puisqu’il n’y en a pas à l’Assemblée, il faut bien qu’il y en ait un au Sénat. »
Voilà, en quelques mots, selon le rapporteur centriste du budget de la Sécu, Olivier Henno, l’objectif que s’est fixé la majorité sénatoriale pour les prochains jours. Après son rejet par les députés, l’examen du texte par les sénateurs est prévu du lundi 9 au mercredi 18 novembre et sera marqué par un vote solennel sur l’ensemble du texte.
Pour la majorité sénatoriale de la droite et du centre, le chemin vers le retour à l’équilibre des comptes sociaux passe, comme l’avait déjà demandé le candidat LR à la présidentielle, Bruno Retailleau, par le retour de la réforme des retraites de 2023, suspendue l’année dernière dans le cadre d’un accord entre le gouvernement et les socialistes.
Opposée à cette suspension, la majorité sénatoriale déposera un amendement pour rétablir la réforme de 2023, de quoi soulager les finances sociales de 600 millions d’euros l’an prochain. « La suppression de la réforme des retraites entre 2026 et 2032 coûtera 10 milliards d’euros en tout. Nous ne pourrons pas continuer à avancer vers le mur, comme c’était lancé », a considéré, hier, la sénatrice LR Marie-Do Aeschlimann (lire notre article).
« Nous devons travailler plus parce que nous vivons plus longtemps et puis aussi parce qu’il y a moins d’actifs pour payer nos retraites. C’est une évidence. Ne pas accepter cette évidence économique, c’est un renoncement qui risque de se traduire par une conséquence concrète : c’est la paupérisation des retraités », a appuyé Olivier Henno au micro de Public Sénat.
La mesure, même adoptée au Sénat, ne devrait pas aller au bout de l’examen du budget, puisque, dépourvu de majorité, le gouvernement devra très probablement avoir recours au 49.3 ou aux ordonnances pour faire passer son budget, dans lequel ne figure pas ce retour de la réforme de 2023. « On ne va tout de même pas voter conforme le projet de loi de financement de la Sécurité sociale qui est proposé par le gouvernement. On va voter un texte qui correspond à nos convictions, à une ligne politique », a-t-il rappelé.

Deux personnes sont mortes noyées dans leur véhicule, dans la nuit de jeudi à vendredi, emportées par une inondation sur la route reliant Bonifacio à Porto-Vecchio (Corse-du-Sud), a annoncé la préfecture de Corse, vendredi 6 novembre.
Trois personnes étaient dans le véhicule mais l’une d’elles a réussi à s’extraire et a été évacuée par hélicoptère vers la clinique de Porto-Vecchio, précise la préfecture alors que la Corse est en vigilance orange pluie-inondations depuis mercredi soir et jusqu’à vendredi midi pour la Corse-du-Sud.
Les secours, dont un plongeur secouriste, sont parvenus à rejoindre le véhicule et à extraire la conductrice d’une cinquantaine d’années, a précisé à l’Agence France-Presse une source proche. Ses parents septuagénaires sont restés coincés dans le véhicule, ont été emportés par les flots et retrouvés morts à bord du véhicule, précise cette source.
Déplacements déconseillés
Depuis mercredi après-midi, un épisode méditerranéen balayant le sud de la France et l’île méditerranéenne a provoqué des évacuations dans le sud de la Corse et des inondations dans la région de Montpellier.
Ces « pluies intenses » se sont abattues sur la région de Porto-Vecchio (Corse-du-Sud) mercredi et jeudi, entraînant, dans la nuit de mercredi à jeudi, la mise en sécurité de plusieurs dizaines de personnes dont une « sauvée par les sapeurs-pompiers qui l’ont sortie de son véhicule emporté par les eaux », avaient précisé les pompiers de Corse-du-Sud.

Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has said he will name a candidate to form the country’s next government by Sunday, after a majority of lawmakers backed opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Herzog made the announcement on Thursday after holding marathon talks with parties elected to the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset.
Some 67 lawmakers endorsed Eisenkot, a former military chief, while 46 backed Netanyahu.
In televised remarks at the end of the talks, Herzog said that although the “results of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the best chance of assembling a governing coalition.
He said he would hold “personal talks with some of the party leaders” over the Israeli weekend, which runs Friday-Saturday, and make a pick on Sunday.
Israel’s October 27 election left neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with a clear path to a parliamentary majority, handing Herzog the difficult task of choosing a candidate in a deeply divided country.
Netanyahu’s Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, but his wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total.
Eisenkot’s alliance of four Jewish-led parties, which spans the political spectrum from centre-left to right, won 48 seats despite polls that had predicted a close race.
Two parties representing Israel’s Palestinian minority won an unprecedented 19 seats.
Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties. Both of those parties nonetheless recommended him, giving him the support of a comfortable majority of lawmakers.
“We want to do things that we did not do in the past in order to remove this criminal government,” Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Joint List, which represents an alliance of Arab parties, told The Associated Press news agency.
Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, said his 67 recommendations were the most any candidate had received since 2015, and urged Herzog to give him the mandate “as soon as possible” so he could form a national emergency government.
Separately, Netanyahu suffered a setback on Thursday when United Torah Judaism, one of the two main ultra-Orthodox parties and a longtime ally, declined to recommend any candidate.
The party broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.
Yariv Oppenheimer, a member of the Democrats, a party in Eisenkot’s alliance, told Al Jazeera that he saw “no reason” Herzog would not choose Eisenkot on Sunday.
He said United Torah Judaism had signalled that its support was available for the right price, meaning that a good enough offer from Eisenkot could give him the numbers he needed.
“It’s very clear that Netanyahu doesn’t have a chance to establish a government at all,” he added.
Once nominated by Herzog, the candidate will have 28 days to try to forge a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
Netanyahu will remain prime minister in a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed, or through another election that must be held if no candidate succeeds.
Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the results, accusing Arab-led parties of stealing the vote.
Critics accuse Netanyahu and his partners of trying to undermine the results, which he denies.
Israel’s Central Election Committee said on Wednesday that the election’s integrity had not been compromised. The head of the committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, has called on Israel’s elected officials to protect public trust rather than shake it.
“This is a real danger. One of the foundations of democracy is the peaceful transfer of power,” Sohlberg told Herzog at his residence on Wednesday. High voter turnout, including among the Arab minority, was a blessing, he said.
Netanyahu’s allies on the far-right, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, have called for the immediate arrest and interrogation of Arab party leaders.

ABSTRACT
When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, standard macroeconomic models and VARs predict 
that output, employment, and inflation should fall over the next several quarters. However, 
monthly-frequency professional macroeconomic forecast revisions are sometimes positively 
correlated with Fed interest rate changes, leading to a debate about what could explain these 
puzzling correlations. We bring to bear new high-frequency data on this question from 
macroeconomic event contracts traded on Kalshi, a CFTC-licensed, U.S.-based event trading 
exchange and prediction market. These high-frequency event contracts allow us to isolate and 
estimate the effects of monetary policy and other announcements on Kalshi market-implied 
macroeconomic expectations. Our results are consistent with standard transmission channels from 
monetary policy to the macroeconomy, with little or no role for a “Fed Information Effect”.

1. Introduction
When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, standard macroeconomic models and VARs
predict that output, employment, and inﬂation should fall over the next several quarters
(e.g., Christiano, Eichenbaum, and Evans , 2005). It is somewhat surprising, then, that
monthly-frequency private-sector professional forecasts of these variables often seem to
respond positively to Federal Reserve interest rate surprises. These puzzling results have
led to a debate in the literature about what might possibly explain them. On the one
hand, the “Fed Information Effect” literature argues that the Fed’s monetary policy surprises
communicate new information to the private sector about the current state of the economy
that the private sector didn’t previously have.(see, e.g., Romer and Romer, 2000; Campbell,
Evans, Fisher , and Justiniano , 2012; Nakamura and Steinsson , 2018). The idea is that
when the Fed raises interest rates, private-sector forecasters infer from that action that the
underlying economy must be stronger than they thought. If this Fed Information Effect is
strong enough, it can even overcome the standard channel of monetary policy transmission
to the economy and lead private-sector forecasters to revise their forecasts in the opposite
direction to what standard macroeconomic models would predict.
More recently , however ,Bauer and Swanson (2023a) argue that these puzzling regres-
sion results are due to the macroeconomic forecast data being available only at a relatively
low , monthly frequency . Over the course of an entire month, a great deal of economic
news is released to the public beyond just the Fed’s monetary policy decision: for exam-
ple, the U.S. Employment Report, CPI report, auto sales, housing starts, etc. are released
every month, and stock market, commodity price, and credit spread data are released
continuously throughout each month. Bauer and Swanson (2023a,b) present substantial ev-
idence that this incoming, publicly available news about the economy and ﬁnancial markets
causes both the Federal Reserve to change interest rates by more than markets expected
and macroeconomic forecasters to revise their predictions for macroeconomic variables. For
example, when incoming news about the economy is stronger than expected, it tends to be
followed both by Federal Reserve monetary policy tightening and by positive private-sector
forecast revisions for GDP, employment, and inﬂation, leading to a positive regression coef-
ﬁcient. Bauer and Swanson refer to this effect as the “Fed Response to News” channel in
monthly-frequency forecast regressions.
In this paper , we present new evidence on this debate in the form of macroeconomic
forecasts that are available at intradaily frequency from Kalshi, a new , U.S.-based event
trading exchange and prediction market that began operating in 2021. In contrast to some
smaller-scale, unlicensed predecessors like Intrade and PredictIt, Kalshi has a license from

institutions and investors to participate in the market, permits those participants to take
much larger positions (up to $7 million per contract), and lets afﬁliated companies act as
liquidity-providing market makers, all of which enhance market functioning and should im-
prove the accuracy of contract prices for predicting future events. 1 We focus in particular
on the most heavily-traded macroeconomic event contracts on the Kalshi exchange: con-
tracts covering the Federal Reserve’s federal funds rate announcements and the U.S. CPI,
GDP, unemployment rate, and nonfarm payrolls releases.
Because the Kalshi macroeconomic event contracts are traded every day (and typically
many times each day), we have access to high-frequency macroeconomic forecast data
that was not available to the authors cited above. Rather than running macroeconomic
forecast response regressions at monthly frequency , we can run those same regressions at
daily frequency and better isolate the effects of monetary policy announcements on the
Kalshi market-implied forecasts of macroeconomic variables like CPI inﬂation, GDP, and
unemployment.

In this paper , we investigate to what extent this ﬁnding is true more generally: When

nature of our Kalshi forecast data allows us to provide new insights into this question.

omitted variables bias story of Bauer and Swanson (2023a,b) and generally not support-

(2000), Campbell et al. (2012), and Nakamura and Steinsson (2018).
Related Literature
Our work is related to two major strands of the literature: studies of prediction markets
and studies of the Fed Information Effect. Gürkaynak and Wolfers (2005) provide an
early survey of prediction markets for macroeconomic data releases in the days before
Kalshi and Polymarket. More recently , Diercks, Katz, and Wright (2026) study the liquidity ,
trading dynamics, accuracy , and distributional properties of the Kalshi market and its
market-implied expectations. Consistent with our results below , they ﬁnd that the Kalshi
market provides a useful and accurate high-frequency measure of macroeconomic forecasts.
3
In contrast to the present paper , they do not study the implications of the Kalshi market
responses for the Fed Information Effect and instead focus on a range of forecasting and
distributional implications. Bürgi, Deng, and Whelan (2026) discuss and model a potential
favorite vs. long-shot bias in the Kalshi market data. Eichengreen, Viswanth-Natraj, Wang,
and Wang (2026) analyze Polymarket data and study how Polymarket participants’ beliefs
about the probability of Fed Chair Powell being removed from ofﬁce is correlated with their
expectations of future U.S. monetary policy and macroeconomic outcomes.
For the Fed Information Effect, Sargent and Wallace (1975) and Barro (1976) present
early theoretical models in which the central bank may possess superior information about
the economy , but Romer and Romer (2000) is the ﬁrst paper to argue that this effect
is empirically important. They ﬁnd evidence that the Fed had information about future
inﬂation that private sector forecasters did not have, and that the Fed’s interest rate changes
could be used to infer some of that information. However , Faust, Swanson, and Wright
(2004) show that FOMC announcements did not signiﬁcantly affect private-sector forecasts
of the very next macroeconomic data releases (e.g., GDP, retail sales, CPI, etc.), while other
macroeconomic data releases such as the employment report, did. They conclude that there
is little evidence of a Fed Information Effect in the data. They also show that the Romer and
Romer (2000) results for inﬂation were due to the Volcker disinﬂation in the early 1980s;
excluding that one episode, the Fed’s inﬂation forecasts were no better than those of the
private sector .
Campbell, Evans, Fisher , and Justiniano (2012) study how Fed monetary policy an-
nouncements affect Blue Chip forecasts of unemployment and inﬂation. They ﬁnd no
evidence that Fed announcements contain signiﬁcant information about inﬂation, but they
do ﬁnd that monetary policy tightenings are associated with a signiﬁcant downward revi-
sion in Blue Chip unemployment rate forecasts, which they attribute to a Fed information
effect. Nakamura and Steinsson (2018) ﬁnd that monetary policy tightenings are associ-
ated with a signiﬁcant upward revision in Blue Chip GDP forecasts, and like Campbell et al.
(2012), appeal to a Fed Information Effect to explain this puzzle.
However ,Bauer and Swanson (2023a) present a variety of evidence against the Fed
Information Effect and in support of their alternative “Fed Response to News” explanation.
In particular , they show that the Fed’s internal Greenbook forecasts are no more accurate
than Blue Chip forecasts, that Blue Chip forecasters do not revise their forecasts in response
to FOMC announcements in a way consistent with a strong Fed Information Effect, and
that previous authors’ results supporting the Fed Information Effect are well explained by
an omitted variables bias due to the omission of major macroeconomic data releases and
4
ﬁnancial market changes from their regressions. Similar to Bauer and Swanson (2023a),
we show here that Kalshi market forecasters also do not generally revise their forecasts in
the way that the Fed Information Effect literature predicts.
Finally ,Jarocinski and Karadi (2020) and Cieslak and Schrimpf (2019) decompose
monetary policy surprises into “pure monetary policy” and “information” shocks, depending
on whether stock prices move in the opposite direction or same direction as interest rates,
respectively .Jarocinski and Karadi (2020) estimate that pure monetary policy shocks are
much more important in the U.S. than information shocks (cf. their Figure 1), that pure
monetary policy shocks cause future GDP to decline, and information shocks cause future
GDP to increase. Cieslak and Schrimpf (2019) ﬁnd a relatively small role for information
shocks in FOMC announcements, but a larger role for those shocks in FOMC minutes
releases and speeches by the Fed Chair . Consistent with these studies, we also ﬁnd at
most a small role for information shocks in FOMC announcements, although we ﬁnd no
evidence of an information effect in Fed Chair speeches and at best only slight evidence of
an information effect in FOMC minutes releases.
Outline of the Paper
The remainder of our paper proceeds as follows. In Section 2, we provide the background
for the Kalshi market and detailed descriptions of the Kalshi market data and describe how
we compute Kalshi market-implied expectations. In Section 3, we show that Kalshi con-
tract trading volumes increase substantially around the times of major monetary policy and
macroeconomic announcements, suggesting that we can get reliable estimates of the effects
of those announcements on the Kalshi market-implied expectations. In Section 4, we con-
duct high-frequency regressions of Kalshi market-implied expectations of macroeconomic
variables on monetary policy announcements and show that those effects are generally con-
sistent with standard macroeconomic models, with no need for a “Fed Information Effect”
to explain the results. In Section 5, we show that high-frequency inﬂation expectations
measures from inﬂation swaps contracts respond to monetary policy announcements very
similarly to the Kalshi market-implied expectations, providing an additional perspective on
our results. We also compare such expectations with alternative decompositions of FOMC
shocks. Section 6 provides additional discussion and Section 7 concludes. An Appendix pro-
vides details of the construction of the market-implied expectations, summary statistics,
and additional results, and an Internet Appendix reports robustness checks.

2. Data and Background
Prediction markets have emerged as a powerful mechanism for aggregating dispersed
information and forecasting future events. Unlike traditional survey-based forecasts that
rely on periodic polling of experts, prediction markets operate continuously and incentivize
accuracy through real monetary stakes. Early prediction markets, such as the Iowa Electronic
Market and Intrade, demonstrated some success in forecasting some political and economic
outcomes, but their scale and liquidity were severely limited by U.S. regulators. The recent
approval of prediction market platforms by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission
(CFTC) represents a very signiﬁcant development, enabling institutional participation, larger
position limits, and professional market-making services that enhance price discovery and
informativeness. This regulatory advancement has created new opportunities for researchers
to study how expectations evolve in real time around important economic events.
Kalshi is a U.S.-based event trading exchange and prediction market that began operating
in July 2021. The term “kalshi” is Arabic for “everything” and, consistent with its name,
the platform offers event contracts across a wide variety of subjects, including economic
data releases, election results, pop culture events, music and ﬁlm awards, sporting event
outcomes, and many others. Unlike previous prediction market alternatives, such as Intrade
and PredictIt, Kalshi has obtained regulatory approval from the U.S. CFTC. This allows
U.S. ﬁnancial institutions to participate on the platform and allows Kalshi to operate on a
much larger scale than competing alternatives—for example, traders on Kalshi can take
positions of up to $7 million in any one contract, while those on the nonproﬁt research
platform PredictIt are limited to a maximum position of $850. 2 Note that Polymarket, the
largest current competitor to Kalshi, did not obtain regulatory approval from the CFTC
until November 2025 and, as a result, was forced to exclude all U.S. investors from trading
on its platform until that point. In general, U.S. investors’ interest in event contracts and
prediction markets has been exploding, with several trading platforms recently announcing
plans to enter the event contract space. 3
One of the advantages of having a CFTC license is that U.S. ﬁnancial institutions can
participate on the platform. T o enhance liquidity in its markets, Kalshi has an afﬁliated

2.1. Event Contracts
Event contracts on Kalshi are generally issued a few months before the corresponding
events and typically have a binary outcome: “yes” or “no”. Each binary contract is a binary
option, offering only two possible payoff outcomes: if the speciﬁc yes-or-no event is true at
expiration, the buyer receives $1; otherwise, the buyer receives nothing. 5
For example, a Federal Funds Rate event contract is a binary contract that settles based
on the upper bound of the Federal Reserve’s target federal funds rate range after a speciﬁed
FOMC meeting. The contracts are written as “Will the target federal funds rate be above
[x]% following the Federal Reserve’s meeting on [date t]?", with the underlying based on
the numbers published on the Federal Reserve’s ofﬁcial website on date t. The contract
expires at the end of date t and settles at the end of that same date. Note that for each
FOMC date t, there are many such Kalshi contracts, one for each different value of x, spaced
0.25 percentage points apart.

6. Discussion
Overall, our estimates in the previous sections are consistent with the standard transmission
mechanisms from monetary policy to the economy in macroeconomic models and VARs,
according to which higher interest rates lead to lower output and employment and lower
inﬂation. Our results thus provide substantial new evidence against the very large Fed
Information Effect that has been proposed by some previous authors (e.g., Romer and
Romer, 2000; Campbell et al. , 2012; Nakamura and Steinsson , 2018) to explain puzzling
positive coefﬁcients in lower-frequency , monthly versions of regression equation ( 5) above.
Previous authors could only estimate lower-frequency versions of regression ( 5) because
standard data on macroeconomic expectations, such as the Blue Chip survey or the Survey of
Professional Forecasters, is only available at a monthly or quarterly frequency . The problem
with running regressions like ( 5) at these lower frequencies is that every month there is a
great deal of macroeconomic and ﬁnancial information released beyond just the Federal
Reserve’s monetary policy announcement. As argued by Bauer and Swanson (2023a,b),
those other macroeconomic and ﬁnancial releases are important omitted variables in
those lower-frequency regressions that seem to be driving the puzzling, positive results
estimated by previous authors. In fact, when Bauer and Swanson (2023a,b) include a
number of the most important omitted variables in a monthly forecast revision regression,
they get a much larger R2, smaller standard errors, and show that the puzzling positive
values for β estimated by previous authors is reversed, making it consistent with standard
macroeconomic models and VARs.
Our use of high-frequency data from Kalshi’s prediction markets has some signiﬁcant ad-
vantages over the data used in these previous studies and provides us with a new perspective
on their results. Unlike the Blue Chip survey or Survey of Professional Forecasters, Kalshi
market-implied expectations are available at a much higher , daily or even intradaily , fre-
39
quency . This high frequency enables us to essentially isolate the effects of speciﬁc economic
events like monetary policy announcements on those Kalshi market-implied expectations
with minimal omitted variables or confounding inﬂuences. As shown in T ables 3 and 4,
Kalshi trading volumes increase substantially around major macroeconomic and monetary
policy announcements, suggesting that market participants actively revise their expecta-
tions in response to new information. Thus, in contrast to Bauer and Swanson (2023a,b),
we don’t even need to control for other variables on the right-hand side of ( 5) because the
narrow , one-day forecast change on the left-hand side already effectively excludes other
macroeconomic and ﬁnancial news releases.
While Bauer and Swanson (2023a,b) run monthly version of regression ( 5) with addi-
tional controls on the right-hand side for macroeconomic and ﬁnancial data, and estimate
negative values of β, we run regression ( 5) at daily frequency—which then requires no ad-
ditional right-hand side controls—and estimate similarly negative values for β. Our results
thus complement those of Bauer and Swanson (2023a,b) and provide supporting evidence
for their ﬁndings from a different perspective.
It’s important to note, however , that these results do not completely rule out all possible
versions of a “Fed Information Effect” more generally . Our evidence here, and that in
Bauer and Swanson (2023a,b), only rules out the extremely strong information effects that
would generate positive coefﬁcients β in regressions like ( 5). More generally , monetary
policy announcements by the Fed could potentially reveal some information about the
state of the economy that the private sector didn’t previously have, but the amount of
that information might be so small that it does not change the sign of the coefﬁcients β
estimated in regression ( 5). Alternatively , the Fed Information Effect might be small on
average—consistent with our estimates above—but might be large on a small number of
isolated dates. This latter version of the Fed Information Effect is the one promoted by
Jarocinski and Karadi (2020) and Lunsford (2020), and our results here, and those in Bauer
and Swanson (2023a,b), do not completely rule that possibility out. However , our results in
T able8 did present some evidence that calls Jarocinski and Karadi’s interpretation of their
speciﬁc “information shock” estimates into question.
7. Conclusions
We use high-frequency data from macroeconomic event contracts traded on Kalshi to
investigate how monetary policy announcements affect market-implied expectations of
macroeconomic variables. We show ﬁrst that Kalshi forecasts have RMSEs comparable to,
and often below , the lower-frequency Blue Chip and Survey of Professional Forecasters
40
benchmarks. Moreover , we show that the Kalshi markets are sufﬁciently liquid to provide
meaningful high-frequency signals regarding macroeconomic expectations, with trading
volumes spiking signiﬁcantly around relevant macroeconomic data releases and monetary
policy announcements. The high-frequency nature of the Kalshi market data—with typi-
cally many trades per event per day—allows us to more directly test competing theories of
monetary policy transmission to the macroeconomy . This constitutes a signiﬁcant method-
ological advancement and a new perspective in the literature estimating monetary policy’s
effects on macroeconomic expectations and the macroeconomy .
Our ﬁndings support the standard transmission channels from monetary policy to
the economy , consistent with standard macroeconomic models and VARs—that is, higher
interest rates cause output, employment, and inﬂation to fall—and are not consistent with
the “Fed Information Effect” literature that predicts opposite signs for these effects (e.g.
Romer and Romer, 2000; Campbell et al. , 2012; Nakamura and Steinsson , 2018).
Although Bauer and Swanson (2023a) present substantial evidence against this strong
Fed Information Effect story , our approach in this paper is more direct. Here, we directly
regress high-frequency , daily changes in market-implied expectations of macroeconomic
variables on interest rate changes around monetary policy announcements, so we are
able to exclude from our regressions all of the macroeconomic and ﬁnancial confounding
factors that Bauer and Swanson (2023a,b) argued were contaminating the monthly- or
quarterly-frequency regressions studied by previous authors and driving the puzzling
positive coefﬁcients in their results. Our results highlight the efﬁcacy of high-frequency data
in clarifying the immediate impacts of monetary policy on macroeconomic expectations,
thereby contributing to a better understanding of the transmission channels of monetary
policy .
The direct nature of our regressions obviates the need to control for omitted economic
news, a common limitation of monthly- or quarterly-frequency analyses. By examining
expectation changes in the immediate vicinity of monetary policy announcements, we
provide a cleaner identiﬁcation of policy effects than has been possible in most previous
studies, provident an alternative and perhaps more convincing resolution of the ongoing
debate on how monetary policy affects private-sector macroeconomic expectations.

When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the

responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of 
the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this 
growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 
11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when 
the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might 
reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate 
rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. 
Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact. In 
my benchmark calibration, hand-to-mouth households lose the equivalent of two-fifths to two-
thirds of their consumption, while keeping them on trend temporarily costs at most a fifth of GDP.

1 Introduction
Artificial intelligence and automation may reshape the economy over the coming decades
(Trammell and Korinek, 2026). Such a transformation will require a great deal of capital: soft-
ware, data centers, robots, power plants, and much else. Van Nieuwerburgh (2026) estimates
that AI campuses alone will absorb 3.6% of GDP per year over 2025–2032, and much of that
capital will depreciate quickly, perhaps not physically but in economic terms.1 Who will save for
the machines?
The answer depends on two margins. The first margin is the task structure of production:
which tasks machines can perform, how productive they are at them, and how substitutable
tasks are for one another. In other words, the task structure governs the returns to accumulating
machines. The second margin is the supply of capital: how much households are willing to save
in response to the returns that machines generate. Capital supply determines how quickly the
economy exploits the existing technological opportunities. But the saving response is ambiguous
ex ante: expectations of higher future income encourage consumption today, while higher future
returns induce more saving.
I model capital supply with a representative household that saves optimally. In the long
run, the supply of capital is perfectly elastic: the return the household requires depends on
consumption growth, not on how much capital it holds. I compare my optimizing economy with
one in which the saving rate is fixed. Thus, I provide two polar cases for the saving response.
Other environments, such as models with household heterogeneity or financial frictions, generate
intermediate responses because their supply of capital has positive but finite elasticity.
Holding the path of automation and machine productivity fixed, the economy grows at 11.7%
a year when tasks are highly complementary and households save optimally, but at only 2.2%
if the saving rate remains at the calibrated 2025 rate of 23%. What looks like a technological
bottleneck under strong task complementarity can reflect insufficient capital accumulation.
The key to this result is that automation raises the capital share by moving tasks from labor
to machines. In comparison, ordinary technical progress makes labor and existing machines
better at the tasks they already perform and, in the Cobb–Douglas case, leaves the capital share
unchanged.2

share times the ratio of investment to capital income. If I take the evolution of the capital share

In my numerical exercises, the capital share rises from one-third to one under full automation,
whereas the ratio of investment to capital income moves only from 0.69 to about 0.55 while the
return climbs from 11% to 52%. In the U.S. data, too, the ratio has stayed between 0.50 and
0.78 since 1950. Thus, apart from its jump on impact, the model’s path for the ratio stays within
the historical range.
The model.The production side of the model is the task framework of Acemoglu and
Restrepo (2018, 2022): output is a CES aggregate of tasks and each task is performed by labor
or by machines, and the task structure collapses into a reduced-form production function in
capital and labor. With symmetric tasks and a Cobb–Douglas aggregator, Imas and Moll (2026)
show that this reduced form has two regimes, which they call cost parity and capital cheaper.
I extend their result: if machines have the same comparative advantage in every task they can
perform, the two regimes survive for any elasticity of substitution across tasks, even when labor
and machines improve at different rates and tasks differ in productivity and weight. When the
comparative advantage of machines differs across tasks, the two regimes merge into one.
With a constant, limited automatable set and constant machine productivity, the model be-
haves like the neoclassical growth model with a Cobb–Douglas production function: the economy
has a balanced growth path (BGP), and local convergence to it is faster the stronger the com-
plementarity across tasks. With a fixed, limited automatable set but continuously improving
machine productivity andσ <1, there is no fixed BGP. Instead, the economy remains close to
the BGP implied by current machine productivity, but with the gap shrinking over time. Along
the way, the capital share and the saving rate fall toward zero: better machines make capital
cheap, not dominant. Under full automation, production becomes linear in capital, as in Ace-
moglu and Restrepo (2018); with common comparative advantage, the model takes the form of
an AK economy with a labor-income endowment and a closed-form solution. The saving rate
converges to the IES, exactly so when machines keep improving and within a few points of the
IES when they do not.

Quantitative results.I calibrate the model to the U.S. economy and compute the tran-
sition to full automation, with every task becoming automatable between 2025 and 2045. In
my benchmark calibration, the optimizing household eventually saves more than half of output.
With a unit elasticity of substitution across tasks,σ= 1, and the benchmark IES of one-half,
households save 15% of output on impact and 54% in the limit; with log utility, the numbers are
52% and 93%; with an IES of one-third, 10% and 41%. A fixed saving rate, by contrast, delivers
a growth boom only above a threshold that rises with task complementarity: 23% clears it with
σ= 1, where growth in 2045 is then 6.5% instead of 22%, but not withσ= 0.2.
While endogenous saving fuels the growth boom,σshapes the transition. Withσ= 1, the
prospect of a richer future dominates and consumption jumps 10% when the automation path
becomes known. Withσ= 0.2, the higher return to saving dominates and consumption falls 9%.
But output rises far above its no-automation trend in both cases: by 2045 it is about sixteen
times trend withσ= 1 and five times trend withσ= 0.2. Wages, however, remain between a
quarter and a half of trend under common comparative advantage, because under full automation
labor cannot earn more than the cost of the machines that replace labor.
Under partial automation, the task structure determines how long the growth boom lasts.
With 85% of the tasks labor performs today becoming automatable, the economy resembles the
fully automated one until about 2040. What happens after that depends onσ. Withσ= 1, the
economy behaves like an AK economy for a century, and growth remains above 12% in 2065.
Withσ= 0.2, growth returns to near 2% by 2065, and the saving rate falls back toward its
initial level, reaching 32% in 2065 and 29% on the new BGP.
Withσ= 0.2, the tasks that remain with labor eventually become the bottleneck. Their
scarcity rents are large: after falling to little more than a quarter of trend in 2040, the wage
rises to nine times trend. For long-run labor income, whether the last tasks are automated is
therefore the key distinction. This is Ricardo’s rent in a new dress: tasks that only labor can
perform become a factor in fixed supply (Ricardo, 1817). Full automation escapes this logic
because the interest rate remains pinned down by machine productivity net of depreciation, so
the gains accrue to capital.
The full-automation wage result depends on machines having a common comparative advan-
tage. When comparative advantage differs across tasks, machines take the tasks they do best
first; as they move to worse tasks, the return to capital falls, while labor retreats to the tasks
where machines perform worst and earns scarcity rents even under full automation. The growth
boom barely changes, but the wage recovers. Withσ= 0.2, the wage bottoms between 0.43 and
0.63 of trend instead of 0.28, and with enough dispersion it eventually returns to trend. Common
comparative advantage is, thus, a knife-edge for the wage, but not for saving or growth.
4
In summary: under full automation, the task structure sets the long-run return to capital
for allσ, and capital supply determines how fast the economy grows; under partial automation,
preferences pin the long-run interest rate, and the task structure determines whether the gains
accrue to capital or labor. Along the transition, capital supply shapes the speed of the growth
boom and the task structure shapes the path of wages.
Welfare and distribution.The welfare gains from automation are large. To be as well off
without automation, the representative household’s consumption would need to grow at about
5% to 10.5% a year, rather than the 1.62% in the pre-automation BGP. Much of that gain comes
from optimal saving. Withσ= 0.2, automation is equivalent to a 109% increase in consumption
at every date with optimal saving, but only 26% when the saving rate remains at 23%.
These welfare gains accrue to the representative household as a whole, even though under
full automation its labor income falls to half of trend or less. To study distribution, I split the
household into two groups: hand-to-mouth households, which consume their labor income and
hold no assets, and owners, who hold all the capital and save optimally. Under full automation,
this split leaves the long run unchanged because labor income vanishes relative to output, and it
slows the transition only slightly. But the gains are no longer shared: hand-to-mouth households
lose the equivalent of 40% to 65% of their consumption, while owners gain even more than the
representative household.
Since output grows much faster than the wage falls relative to trend, the transfer required to
keep labor income on trend is small relative to output: it peaks at 4% of GDP withσ= 1 and
20% withσ= 0.2, and it is below 4% by 2055 in both cases. Furthermore, financing this transfer
with a tax on capital income has modest growth costs: growth falls by at most 1.1 percentage
points withσ= 1 and 3.3 points withσ= 0.2, and not at all in the long run.
Prices and wealth.I also look at asset prices. When the automation path starts, the
short rate does not move: the stock of machines is given. But a ten-year bond competes with
the machines that will be built over the next ten years, and those machines will earn 25% to
46%. So the ten-year real yield jumps on impact from 5.1% to 13.6% withσ= 1 and to 9.3%
withσ= 0.2, and the thirty-year yield to 33.0% and 19.6%.
The same high rates cut the value of the labor force by two-thirds on impact: the start of
automation does to human wealth what a permanent rate hike does to a long bond. The stock
market, however, does not move on impact, because market value equals the capital stock and
machines earn no rents. The boom in the market is a boom in quantities: under full automation,
market value grows at 10% to 16% a year in 2035, while the price-earnings ratio falls from 20 to
between 2 and 4 by 2045.

Related literature.The production side of my model traces back to Zeira (1998): ma-
chines replace labor task by task. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018) built the modern task frame-
work around this idea and already embedded it in a dynamic model with representative-household
saving and endogenous capital accumulation. They characterize balanced growth paths, includ-
ing full automation, and also study the adjustment of capital when automation runs ahead of
the creation of new tasks. I take the paths of automation as given and focus on how the saving
response changes the transition along those paths. Full automation also appears in Aghion et al.
(2019), where Baumol’s cost disease keeps growth bounded as the automated share approaches
one. Jones and Tonetti (2026) calibrateσ= 0.2 and find a slow acceleration from AI. I show
that, with optimal saving, that slow acceleration becomes double-digit growth.
Imas and Moll (2026) put this technology into a Solow model and compute a transition
with growth above 10% within a decade and a labor share that converges to zero. I keep their
automation path and two regimes, extending the latter toσ̸= 1, but let the household choose
saving optimally along the transition. Imas and Moll note that under full automation a log-
utility household would save 1−0.047/Rof output, the limit in Proposition 17; my focus is on
how this endogenous saving response interacts with the task structure throughout the transition.
Farboodi et al. (2026) obtain explosive growth from the interaction of endogenous data and
capital accumulation: data raises machine productivity and expands the automation frontier,
so even a fixed positive saving rate can generate a growth explosion. While their mechanism
operates through endogenous technological change, I take the automation path as given.
The literature models saving in different ways. In overlapping-generations models, saving
comes out of wages, so automation that depresses wages chokes off investment: Sachs and Kot-
likoff (2012) and Benzell et al. (2015) get immiseration, and Gasteiger and Prettner (2022) show
that an AK production side may fail to deliver long-run growth. Berg et al. (2018) let only
capitalists and skilled labor save and find real wages falling for generations. An infinitely lived
household is the opposite benchmark: since labor and capital income are fungible, the saving rate
can ultimately rise sharply as capital income expands (Propositions 10 and 17). Moll et al. (2022)
are closest to my emphasis on capital supply. Their supply of capital slopes upward, so automa-
tion raises the return to wealth, by a margin that grows with the capital share, and benefits those
who already own it. They contrast this case with the perfectly elastic representative-household
benchmark. In their growing economy, however, long-run growth is driven by exogenous pro-
ductivity growth; here, once automation becomes sufficiently extensive, the saving response can

change the growth rate itself.
Optimal saving when machines replace labor is much older than the current debate over AI.
Steigum (2011) obtains endogenous growth without scale effects when robot capital is a close
substitute for labor, as in my case with ˆ︁ψk = 0, and Prettner (2019) gets perpetual growth
without technological progress in a Solow model with automation capital. Erdil et al. (2025)
solve numerically a planner’s problem in which compute drives automation.
Korinek and Suh (2024) show that wages collapse once machines can perform every task
humans can, and Restrepo (2026) gives the sharpest statement of the limit: with artificial
general intelligence, wages converge to the cost of the compute that reproduces human work. I
obtain the same limit with endogenous saving and add the price of the future stream of wages.
Korinek et al. (2026) also obtain rapid growth and a falling labor share, but do not endogenize
saving or the interest rate. Chow et al. (2025) use long rates to infer market expectations of
transformative AI, while Trammell and Korinek (2026) emphasize that saving may rise or fall
with interest rates.
