Parts (ii) to (iv) of the proposition say that the stock market boom is a quantity boom, not
a valuation boom. The price-earnings ratio,V /(rK) = 1/r, falls from 20 before automation to

to output, the capital-output ratio in my model, ends up between 1.9 and 3.2, compared with 3
in 2025. Capital explodes, but so does output.
The composition of wealth, however, changes drastically. Before automation, equity is only
14% of household wealth and human wealth the remaining 86%. The announcement of automa-
tion alone pushes the equity share to between 31% and 36%, mostly because human wealth falls.
By 2045, under full automation, equity accounts for more than 95% of wealth. Total wealth rela-

44

Table C.1, in Online Appendix C, reports the stock market of Proposition 16 in the twelve

below by 2045 in every one of them. Under partial automation with strong complementarities,
the equity share of wealth rises and then falls back: from 31% on impact to 54% in 2045 and 20%
in 2065 withσ= 0.2, as the wage and human wealth recover, and wealth ends at 18 times GDP,
close to where it started, against 3 under full automation. Under full automation with improving
machines, the market’s value relative to GDP falls below 1.7 by 2065 while the dividend yield
reaches 21% to 35%: the market is worth little relative to what the economy produces and pays
out almost everything it earns.
Adjustment costs.Building a data center requires permits, new skills, and overcoming

Online Appendix A varies one parameter at a time under full automation and constant

Four results stand out. First, as Proposition 8 predicts, the IES and the cost ratioqare the
parameters that matter most quantitatively. The growth boom occurs for everyγ: asγgoes from
1 to 4, limit growth falls from 42% to 12% withσ= 1 and from 22% to 6.6% withσ= 0.2, and
the limit saving rate from 93% to 34% and from 89% to 41%, always above the Solow threshold
of Table 3. The cost ratio moves the wage floor, from 0.37 to 0.58 of trend withσ= 1 asqgoes
from 0.05 to 0.20: how far wages fall under full automation is a matter of calibration.
Second, how fast automation arrives changes how much consumption, saving, and interest
rates jump on impact, not where the economy ends up. The limit growth and saving rates are
the same whether automation takes ten, twenty, or forty years. But the ten-year yield in 2025 is
28% if automation takes ten years and 8% if it takes forty, against 14% in the baseline, where it
takes twenty.
Third, when the capital stock consists of data centers that depreciate at 20% a year,δmatters
more thanσ. Withσ= 0.2, growth falls from 11.6% to 4.6% and the household saves 79% of
output, because replacing the machines alone eats 64% of it. A fixed saving rate of 23% does
not even replace the machines that wear out, and output in 2045 is half of its trend.
Fourth, dispersion in comparative advantage (Section 6.3) and adjustment costs (Section 9.3)
46
leave the growth boom intact: adjustment costs take four to seven points off limit growth with
σ= 1 and one to three withσ= 0.2.
11 Conclusion
I have asked how much the macroeconomic consequences of automation depend on the capital
supplied to exploit it. The answer changes how we should interpret technological bottlenecks to
AI-driven growth. Strong complementarity across tasks can leave growth near its historical rate
when saving remains fixed and still produce double-digit growth when households save optimally.
What looks like a technological bottleneck can therefore be a capital-supply bottleneck: the task
structure determines the returns available from accumulating machines, while capital supply
determines how much of that opportunity the economy exploits.
The distinction between a technological and a capital-supply bottleneck has observable im-
plications. First, the saving rate should track the capital share. Investment as a share of capital
income barely moves in my simulations, from 0.69 to about 0.55, so if the capital share climbs,
investment should climb with it. If investment stays at a fifth of GDP while the capital share
rises, the plow-back ratio must fall sharply, unlike along the optimizing paths of Section 7, and
the Solow benchmark describes the world better. Second, the early years are informative about
σ. Withσ= 1, the start of automation brings a consumption boom, higher wages, and a dip in
saving. Withσ= 0.2, consumption falls at once, saving jumps, and the wage is below trend by
2032. Finally, long real yields should jump on impact while the short rate stays put. Holding
the automation path fixed, the size of the jump is informative about the saving response: with
a fixed saving rate andσ= 0.2, there is no growth boom and long yields barely move. On the
other hand, the data will not tell us for decades whether the last tasks will be automated and
whether the interest rate will return toρ+γg.
The main thrust of my results rests on a sufficiently elastic supply of capital, and many
mechanisms can cap that elasticity: heterogeneous agents, financial frictions, and limited phys-
ical resources. Of all of them, I am intrigued by heterogeneous agents. The hand-to-mouth
households of Section 8.2 are a first step, with the ownership of capital fixed; a model in which
it moves is the natural next step. Other forms of capital deserve attention too, housing above
all. Beachfront lots in Montecito will be the same with or without automation. If automation
multiplies output by a factor of 100, I wonder what those lots will fetch in 2126.
And then there is political economy, probably the most important omission of my analysis.
A wage that falls to a quarter of trend for two decades is unlikely to be greeted with unremitting
merriment by the median voter. The equilibrium path studied here therefore describes what
the technology and the supply of capital permit, not necessarily what political institutions will
allow.

Outils de rejeu de session : la CNIL publie sa recommandation pour guider les acteurs
05 novembre 2026
La CNIL publie une recommandation relative aux outils de rejeu de session permettant le suivi et l'analyse du comportement en ligne des utilisateurs. L’objectif est d’aider les acteurs qui conçoivent ces outils et ceux qui les utilisent dans leur mise en conformité.
Les enjeux
Les outils de rejeu de session fonctionnent avec des traceurs et servent à enregistrer visuellement ou à reconstituer le parcours complet de navigation d’un internaute sur un site web ou une . Ils peuvent notamment être utilisés pour détecter et corriger des dysfonctionnements, ou encore optimiser la structure ou l’ergonomie d’un service numérique.
Concrètement, ces outils offrent à l’éditeur d’un site ou d’une application mobile la possibilité d’enregistrer l’ensemble des interactions des utilisateurs : mouvements de souris, interactions tactiles, clics, défilement des pages et, dans certains cas, saisies dans les formulaires. Ces éléments sont ensuite utilisés pour analyser le parcours de l’internaute sous forme de vidéos.
Si ces solutions offrent de nouvelles possibilités de suivi et d’analyse des comportements des internautes, elles présentent également des risques élevés d’atteinte à la vie privée de ces derniers. Elles peuvent notamment conduire à collecter des données personnelles qui ne sont pas nécessaires à l’analyse recherchée.
Une recommandation pour encadrer l’utilisation des outils de rejeu de session
À qui s’adresse-t-elle ?
La recommandation de la CNIL s’adresse à deux catégories d’acteurs :
- les fournisseurs d’outils de rejeu de session, qui conçoivent les solutions techniques et définissent les paramétrages et fonctionnalités ;
- les éditeurs de sites web ou d’applications mobiles, qui déploient ces outils pour analyser les parcours de leurs utilisateurs.
Quels sont ses objectifs ?
La recommandation apporte des réponses concrètes aux enjeux juridiques et techniques liés à l’utilisation des outils de rejeu de session. Elle vise à aider les fournisseurs et les éditeurs à respecter le principe de des données et à déterminer les conditions dans lesquelles ces solutions peuvent déployées.
Elle explicite notamment les obligations relatives à l’information des personnes et la manière de recueillir leur consentement. Elle propose également des recommandations techniques et organisationnelles qui doivent permettre aux fournisseurs qui proposent ces outils et aux éditeurs qui les exploitent de s’assurer du respect de la règlementation applicable.
Les principaux apports de la recommandation
Clarifier le rôle des acteurs et le cadre juridique applicable
La recommandation aide les acteurs à déterminer leur qualification en fonction de leur rôle et en lien avec le cadre légal applicable. Elle précise que les outils de rejeu de session fonctionnent avec des traceurs et qu’ils doivent respecter les dispositions de l’article 82 de la loi Informatique et Libertés.
La recommandation rappelle que ces outils sont soumis au consentement préalable des personnes, puisqu’aucune exemption prévue par cet article n’est applicable. Le recueil du consentement doit donc respecter les règles déjà exposées par la CNIL en matière de traceurs (cookies).
Préciser les finalités pour lesquelles les outils peuvent être déployés
La recommandation rappelle que les outils de rejeu de session doivent être utilisés pour des finalités déterminées, explicites et légitimes. Ces finalités doivent être déterminées en amont du déploiement des outils, et non après la collecte des données.
Proposer des recommandations concrètes aux acteurs
La recommandation propose aux acteurs une série de mesures techniques et opérationnelles, adaptables aux finalités poursuivies, afin de s’assurer de la conformité de ces outils aux principes clés du RGPD.
Elle souligne l’importance de mettre en place un outil de masquage permettant d’occulter les données non pertinentes, de limiter le nombre de sessions collectées en fonction des finalités poursuivies et de limiter le recours aux identifiants.
Une recommandation enrichie par la consultation publique
Cette recommandation a fait l’objet d’échanges avec des professionnels et des associations représentatives de la société civile. Elle a également été soumise à consultation publique entre février et mai 2026. Les contributions reçues ont permis de mieux comprendre les usages et les enjeux de ces outils.
La CNIL a apporté plusieurs clarifications dans cette version finale :
- La recommandation apporte aux acteurs des précisions sur le contenu de l’information à fournir en distinguant les informations de premier et deuxième niveau des interfaces de recueil du consentement. La recommandation propose des formulations pour parvenir à cet objectif.
- La version définitive du document prévoit désormais une recommandation relative à l’information spécifique sur l’utilisation de ces outils, à fournir dès le premier niveau des interfaces utilisées afin de s’assurer du recueil d’un consentement éclairé.
- Enfin, elle ajoute une précision dans les mesures techniques proposées en recommandant le masquage des mouvements de souris dans certaines zones afin d’éviter la collecte incidente de codes d’authentification.
- La recommandation couvre les risques associés à l’usage d’outils de rejeu utilisés dans des chatbots (agents conversationnels). Elle précise que ces outils devraient permettre de masquer le contenu des discussions (questions et réponses), celles-ci pouvant révéler des données potentiellement sensibles.
Les prochaines étapes
La CNIL accompagnera les acteurs professionnels, notamment à travers un webinaire. L’objectif est que les professionnels s’approprient au mieux les règles et les recommandations présentées dans la recommandation et qu’ils puissent mettre en œuvre les mesures proposées pour assurer leur conformité.

The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) filed plans Thursday to extend the one-year suspension of its Affiliates Rule, also known as its 50% rule, through Jan. 10.
The Trump administration’s pause on the rule, which would significantly expand the scope of American export controls by covering majority-owned subsidiaries of parties named on the BIS Entity List and certain other blacklists, had been set to end Monday.
The White House had initially moved to delay the Affiliates Rule last November, as part of a trade deal with China that included Beijing shelving export controls on rare earth minerals. The notice of the two-month extension, set to publish in the Federal Register  on Monday, did not provide an explanation, though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had signaled the action was coming in September, citing ongoing efforts to secure a broader bilateral deal with China. 
BIS’s press office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
The Affiliates Rule, when it arrived last fall, stood to close an export-control loophole that had long been discussed inside the Commerce Department and long anticipated outside it. Government and military officials have increasingly expressed concern about the diversion of advanced tech and other dual-use goods, particularly to China, through non-blacklisted subsidiaries.
“For too long, loopholes have enabled exports that undermine American national security and foreign policy interests,” Jeffrey Kessler, undersecretary of commerce for industry and security, said in a statement after the rule’s September 2025 rollout. “Under this Administration, BIS is closing the loopholes and ensuring that export controls work as intended.”
Besides the Entity List, the rule would also apply to subsidiaries owned 50% or more, whether directly or indirectly, by parties on the Military End-User List or by certain parties on U.S. sanctions lists.
A Kharon analysis last year found that thousands of subsidiaries — in nearly 100 jurisdictions across six continents — would fall under export-control regulations if such an ownership rule were enacted.
But the Affiliates Rule became a flashpoint with Beijing even before its restrictions took effect, and it quickly became a bargaining chip in trade negotiations between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Rare earths, as critical components in everything from high-tech defense systems to consumer electronics, represent a strategic vulnerability and chokepoint for much of the West because of China’s dominance over the global market. 
Experts told The Brief after the rule’s post-summit suspension that the volatility of the U.S.-China dynamic made it difficult to predict what could come next. 
A White House fact sheet at the time, however, had hinted at additional delays, stating that the Affiliates Rule would go into effect Nov. 9, 2026, “absent a future extension.”

The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.
That is according to Carbon Brief’s latest “state of the climate” update, which analyses El Niño forecasts from more than a dozen climate models, as well as six global temperature datasets.
Dr Zeke Hausfather, Carbon Brief’s climate science contributor, described this year’s El Niño as “simply staggering” when answering questions from CB+ members during a CB Connect “ask me anything” session.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere and temporarily boosts global temperatures.
This year’s El Niño event – which has been underway since June – has already broken a number of records and reshaped the world’s weather, fuelling fires in Indonesia and “super typhoons” in the west Pacific.
The strength of an El Niño is tracked using the “Niño3.4 anomaly”, which is a measure of how much warmer sea surface temperatures are than average in a section of the central Pacific.
Analysis of more than 600 forecasts from 14 different climate models by Hausfather for Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” update shows how models project this year’s El Niño will peak with an anomaly of around 4C. This would be more than a degree above the previous record in 2015-16.
Writing on CB Connect on 5 November, Hausfather wrote:
“This El Niño event is developing so quickly and is reaching sea surface temperatures so warm that it’s simply staggering. We haven’t seen anything like this in the historical record and it may end up being the strongest El Niño event in the past millennium.”
This year’s El Niño has already chalked up a number of milestones.
On 18 September, the daily anomaly in the Niño3.4 region broke the satellite-era record set in 2015 when it reached 3.11C.
Meanwhile, September as a whole recorded the highest monthly Niño3.4 region temperature anomaly – 2.84C – since sea surface temperature records began in the mid-1800s.
Membership
Support award-winning climate journalism
Hausfather wrote on CB Connect that this year’s El Niño had been “running well above any prior El Niño event since June, at times by a full degree [Celsius]”.
Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” analysis indicates that El Niño is set to continue to intensify into December, with 10 out of 14 models expecting temperatures in the Niño3.4 region to peak in the final month of this year. The remainder anticipate a November peak.
While human emissions of greenhouse gases are responsible for almost all of long-term global warming, temperatures in specific years are strongly influenced by El Niño events.
The “state of the climate” analysis explains that this year’s El Niño event will have its largest effect on global temperatures in 2027. This is because global temperatures typically lag warming in the tropical Pacific by around three months.
Carbon Brief projects that the 2027 average global temperature will reach around 1.74C above pre-industrial levels. It calculates a 96% chance that next year will be the warmest on record.
This projection is based on the historical relationship between year-on-year temperature changes and El Niño conditions the preceding autumn. It also factors in uncertainty around how global temperatures will develop across the remainder of 2026.

China’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions fell by 3.1% in the third quarter of 2026, as the Hormuz crisis continued to hit oil demand and coal use also dropped.
This guest post is by:
Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air
This was the largest quarterly reduction since the 2022 Covid lockdowns and means that China’s CO2 emissions have now fallen by an estimated 0.5% in the year to date.
The new analysis for Carbon Brief, based on official figures and commercial data, shows that coal use fell by 3% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, while oil was down 4%.
The main drivers were a fall in power-sector coal consumption, a continued sharp reduction in transport oil consumption and slowing growth in the coal-to-chemical industry.
The sharp decline in China’s CO2 emissions extends a “flat or falling” trend that began in March 2024 and has now lasted more than two years, as shown in the figure below.
The outlook for China’s CO2 emissions depends on the balance between rising energy demand, clean-energy growth and the government response to a GDP slowdown.
Decline drivers
Key drivers of the fall in CO2 in the third quarter of 2026 included a 3.3% drop in coal-power generation, after demand growth slowed and the amount of “wasted” wind and solar fell.
Power generation from solar, wind and nuclear increased by 110 terawatt hours (TWh) year-on-year, more than twice as much as the growth in total electricity demand. This added clean-power generation equal to Germany’s total power output in the same time period.
The fall in coal-power output and CO2 emissions came despite the fact that China continues to build new coal-power capacity at near-record rates. This means that average running hours for coal plants are falling even faster than total generation, eroding their profits.
Meanwhile, transport oil consumption continued to fall sharply, down 9% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026. Electric vehicles (EVs) continued to gain market share, hitting a record 67% of passenger car sales and 50% of heavy trucks in September.
The amount of electricity used by EVs grew by 53%, much faster than the number of EVs on the road, showing increased usage of the existing fleet in preference to fuelled vehicles.
Elsewhere, growth in the coal-to-chemical industry continued to slow down in the third quarter of 2026. The sector has been a key source of emissions growth, but high coal prices have weakened profitability and higher output prices hurt downstream demand.
Finally, CO2 emissions from cement and steel production continued to fall in the third quarter, as the contraction in construction volumes accelerated.
Outlook for emissions
Energy consumption growth has been falling after a period of exceptionally high growth during Covid, while clean-power growth has been robust.
This makes it likely that the growth in clean-power generation will exceed total energy demand growth this year, maintaining the structural fall in fossil-fuel use.
Looking ahead, this balance also relies on progress in removing barriers to new solar and wind power being added to the grid, which result in some clean electricity being “wasted”.
The recent slowdown in energy demand growth is partly – but not fully – explained by exceptionally mild weather in the third quarter.
Another key factor is weaker GDP growth. Since reported GDP growth remains within target, however, there is reduced pressure for further stimulus policies.
The focus of the economic stimulus announced to date is “six networks”, which includes the power grid and the transportation network.
These networks are highly relevant for energy and emissions – and they are already covered by policies that emphasise “green” and zero-carbon solutions.
